Since there are no definite plans to prepare the Canadian Sault locks for deep sea draught vessels, can we assume that the United States locks at the Sault are to be the future passageway of such vessels going to and from lake Superior?
The answer is that the Canadian Sault Ste. Marie lock was enlarged to its present dimensions of 60 feet in width, 900 feet in length and normal draught of 18 feet 3 inches between the years 1887 and 1895. The United 96698-424
Inquiries of the Ministry States locks were built progressively and afford deeper draught than ours, and have been used as required by Canadian shipping drawing too much water or of greater size than could be accommodated through the Canadian lock.

In view of the adequacy of the United States locks it has not been felt necessary to duplicate, at a very substantial cost to the taxpayers, the facilities at the Sault. maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an answer now for the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and other hon.

Inquiries of the Ministry members who asked questions concerning the proposed visit of our trade commissioner to China.
China is part of the trade promotion territory of our trade commissioner in Hong Kong, and in the course of his normal duties he is expected and required to visit all parts of his territory. In December, 1955, China was listed as falling within the responsibility of Canada's trade commissioner in Hong Kong. The proposed visit to China is, therefore, in no sense a trade mission but rather an exploratory trip by an officer through a part of his territory.
A year ago, following the successful visit to China of the Australian trade commissioner in Hong Kong, our trade commissioner reported fully to the Department of Trade and Commerce and at the same time suggested the desirability of a similar visit by himself. This was taken under advisement, and during the course of the year an exchange of correspondence took place between the head office in Ottawa and the trade commissioner in Hong Kong, in an attempt to determine whether the present would be an appropriate time to undertake a visit to China. In view of the increasing interest in China by Canadian and other businessmen the officials of the department decided to recommend an exploratory visit.
Mr. Forsyth-Smith will be accompanied by Mr. T. M. Pope as an assistant trade commissioner. The officials will carry no credentials beyond the customary diplomatic passports provided all trade commissioners. Mr. Forsyth-Smith and his assistant are planning to leave Hong Kong about November 5. On their return to Hong Kong the trade commissioner will report fully on trade possibilities and it is, of course, to be hoped that his visit will uncover opportunities for the sale of additional non-strategic products in China.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
May
I ask a supplementary question. The minister said the officials would carry Canadian passports. What provision is made for obtaining visas from the government of the Chinese mainland; because I presume the government of the Chinese mainland will require visas, as other countries do? What provision is being made to secure them?

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: The trade commissioner has made those arrangements. maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: The question of strategic materials has been discussed in the House of Commons on many occasions in the last few years, but certainly non-strategic materials would be foodstuffs such as wheat, and that is the main interest at the present time. Hon. members may have noticed that a serious crop situation has developed in China recently, and there is grave danger of starvation of many of the Chinese people. If hon. members are interested there is an article in the current issue of Time which deals with that matter.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
May I
ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question. In view of the fact that public funds are being spent to send a delegation to China, will the Prime Minister reconsider the question of recognizing the government on the mainland in the hope that we may extend our exports?

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the experience of the United Kingdom, which recognized communist China prior to the Korean war, has added little to the extension or expansion of trade between that country and communist China. There is nothing inconsistent about endeavouring to trade and at the same time not recognizing the government of that country. The attitude of this government is unchanged in that direction, and until such time as the people's government, the communist government of China, expiates its wrongdoing under international law there certainly will be no justification for the granting of recognition, as we see it.
Recognition under international law in the past used to be a juridical act, but today the information we have indicates that recognition would be regarded by various countries in Asia which have withstood communism as an act of more than legal recognition and, indeed, would be interpreted as a recognition of communism as such and would afford to those who today resist communism the removal of a major incentive that has impelled them to take their stand firmly against the onrush of communism throughout portions of Asia.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
I should like to ask a supplementary question. The Prime Minister has said that if the so-called Chinese people's republic expiated its crimes, then his government would give consideration. Does he mean by expiation that if they undid their participation in the Korean war

the government would do so, or does he wish to add to that the reasons which the government of the United States has given as well?

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in no way accepting the interpretation of my remarks as placed thereon by the hon. member for Essex East, may I say that our stand is unchanged with regard to recognition. It might be epitomized in the words of a former prime minister of this country, paraphrasing those words to apply them to the present circumstances: not necessarily recognition but recognition when necessary.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: If necessary.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: In other words the matter is subject to constant revision, but there is no purpose, intentionally or otherwise, at this time or in the immediate foreseeable future, to bring about recognition.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: In view of the importance of this question could the Prime Minister be more precise as to what he means exactly by "expiation"?

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: Look it up in a dictionary.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: I have asked the Prime Minister a question and he has not replied. I take it he does not intend to answer a very important question.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend can look up the dictionary definition of expiation, and I am sure under those circumstances he will have a full answer.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. If the Prime Minister feels that recognition of the government of the Chinese mainland might imply approval, would he say that diplomatic recognition of the U.S.S.R. implies any measure of approval on the part of the Canadian government?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: Order. This seems to be developing into an argument or debate. In view of the rather important statement which the Prime Minister has made I am quite prepared to have comments, but I think the hon. member for Regina City will be willing to let that question stand.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is a matter arising out of the answer given by the Prime Minister, and I believe it is a very important point. If the Prime Minister feels that diplomatic recognition involves some measure of approval, how does he justify the fact that Canada today recognizes quite a number of countries whose governments
Inquiries of the Ministry certainly by no stretch of the imagination could be considered acceptable to the Canadian people?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: My point, and I would ask the hon. member for Regina City to consider it, is that I do not feel we should now enter into a debate on foreign policy, and that is what we would do if we pursued this line of questions and answers. In view of the fact that the Prime Minister did make a lengthy and important statement I said I was prepared to hear briefly spokesmen for the official opposition and the other parties, but I do not think I should admit questions of an argumentative type.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce a supplementary question. Since the government has taken office has the minister or the government received any representations from or had any communications with any parties in Canada regarding the possible sale of wheat in China?

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: I am not aware of any representations made to the government with respect to the question asked by the hon. member.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, some time ago I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce about the proposed visit to Japan, widely publicized in the press, of Mr. Ezra Benson, United States secretary of agriculture, and the acceptance of Japanese currency for United States wheat, such currency to be invested in Japan. Has the minister made any investigation of the matter, and what steps does he propose to take in order that we may safeguard the market which we have promoted in Japan?

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not quite clear as to whether I should keep under surveillance the movements of Mr. Benson.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: I am not suggesting that.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
I think he is entitled to go anywhere he wishes to promote trade between the United States and other countries. This is not the beginning of United States trade with Japan; far from it. The United States has encouraged the consumption of wheat in Japan and is doing so at the present time. Canada has benefited accordingly from that, because as wheat becomes more acceptable in countries where the people are normally rice eating, there is greater prospect of the sale of Canadian wheat.
We are taking no steps with regard to Mr. Benson's visit to Japan. We anticipate that our trade in wheat with Japan will be maintained at its present level. Japan is our

Inquiries of the Ministry third best customer for wheat and we think that trade will be improved, but I cannot quite see the connection between that situation and the visit of Mr. Benson.
Mr. Cold well: May I just give the connection. Recently there was a conference between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other representatives of the Canadian government and the United States government. I understood it was agreed that the United States would discontinue methods of marketing that interfere with Canadian trade. Does the minister consider that the taking of Japanese currency for investment by the United States in that country, in payment for wheat, is in any way carrying out what is believed to be the understanding reached at Washington?

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
The meeting at Washington was certainly very profitable. We achieved complete understanding with the United States representatives concerning their surplus disposal program. The chief damage of the United States surplus disposal program as it affected Canadian sales of wheat was due to their method of bartering wheat for strategic materials, and we have had an assurance from them that this will be discontinued.
Now, there are other methods of disposing of wheat, through sales for local currency, as has been mentioned by the hon. member. This course has been followed where wheat has not, over the years, been accepted by the population. There may be no permanent damage done. The sale of wheat for local currencies has been made by the United States in a number of countries, but I do not see how we can raise any objection to that unless there is an interference with a traditional Canadian market. In this instance I do not think any harm is going to result at all.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: It seems the United States did fix us, then.

May

Our trade commissioner who is visiting Hong Kong will naturally look into all aspects of possible Canadian trade with China and will report to us.
I just caught an interjection, Mr. Speaker, by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, which if I caught it correctly was that the United States did fix us. There was no fixing of the Canadians by the United States repre-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, to assure the hon. member perhaps I might give a little information on what has happened in the past. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, October 31, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Monteith-Mr. Courte-manche in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Old Age Security Act to increase the amount of monthly pensions payable thereunder to fifty-five dollars per month, to reduce the basic residence requirements for pensioners from 20 years to 10 years and to increase the length of permissible temporary absences of pensioners from Canada from three to six months.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we may have expected that this resolution would have passed before last night's adjournment. Since it did not, I take this opportunity of placing before the minister a question. I am doing so now because the answer may involve some statistical research over the next day or two. I am interested particularly in that part of the measure which deals with old age security recipients being able to go to another country and perhaps reside there if they choose to do so. I recognize that the measure is going to extend the period of time during which old age security recipients can be away from Canada from three months to six months. They can be away for six months one year, and if those are the last six months in the year they can be away six months in the following year. This would made an absence of a year. However, they cannot go away again then until the year following that.
We appreciate this extension of time, but I do believe it is not good enough. We have advocated on the floor of this house that if a person resides in Canada for the required length of time to become eligible for old age security and then finds it necessary to go away, he should still be able to leave the country and draw his old age pension.
To some that may not sound too reasonable, but to some of us it is most reasonable. I stated previously on the floor of the house that I had two specific cases which I think merit a good deal of consideration. One of those cases is that of a gentleman who, by reason of his health, apparently must live in
Old Age Security Act
England where he has relatives. This gentleman came to this country when he was a young man, farmed in this country and later set up business in a small community. He reached the age of 70 years and retired, but he retired on a very small amount of money after the sale of his small business and was obliged to go to England. He found that his health was much better there. However he returned again to Canada, desiring to settle once again, but his old malady came back again so he returned to England where he was free from it. The result, of course, was that his old age security pension was cut off.
The other case I have is similar. A gentleman came here in the early days, in the previous century, and homesteaded in Canada. He went through extremely difficult times. He went through the hungry thirties, and in those years he was forced to sell his farm. However, he managed to scrape through. He became 70 years of age, was in receipt of the pension and went back to his old home town in the United States. It so happened that he married there and that his wife did not see fit to come back to Canada. He therefore went to reside there. He has no income apart from the income he may have received from his old age security pension, but it was cut off.
It seems to me that in such cases that treatment is unjust. The man had lived here, had put in his life here, had done something for the country, and yet he finds that he cannot be in receipt of his old age security pension. The situation is accentuated now more than ever because the recipient of old age security pension has been paying into the old age security fund into which we all are obliged to pay. I therefore say that we should extend the provisions of the act to include all those who wish to reside in other countries.
There is another argument I have, and it is this. Under the British pension scheme old age pensioners, after they receive their pension, can come to Canada and live here and the British government still pays their old age pension while they are living here. I want the minister to consider making a further amendment to enable people to receive their pensions even though they live in some other country. The number of those who would leave the country is nominal, I am sure. Most aged people who have put in their lives here, have established their homes here and whose families are here would remain in Canada except in the case of some extenuating circumstances.
My question to the minister is this, and perhaps he would answer it at a later date. I do not expect him to have the figures at

Old Age Security Act his finger tips. I should like to know how many recipients of old age security have been cut off from their pensions by reason of going to some other country to live. I think the figures would be almost infinitesimal compared to the over-all picture. For the life of me I do not see why they are cut off. I would ask the minister to consider that part of the act and bring down those figures for the enlightenment of the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I just say we have been asking for this same thing for a long time, as have many members on all sides of the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: As a matter of fact I think that some of the Conservative members recommended it when they sat over there on the other side.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
That is right. I want to reinforce the argument with regard to the payment of the pension. It is true that the people who are receiving it today are not yet paying a very substantial premium. However, they are paying a premium, and it is therefore paid as of right. But the younger people who are paying sales tax and 2 per cent income tax will, by the time they reach 65 or 70, have paid a substantial premium indeed on an annuity, and they should have it as of right.
The other day, as a matter of fact, I was reading a debate that took place in this house in 1936. The hon. gentleman can look it up. It was on an unemployment measure. Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was speaking and he introduced this very matter in that speech. He said that recently he had been in the Antipodes-and I use his own word. He said that down there a feeling prevailed that there should be some reciprocity between the various members of the commonwealth such as, for example, New Zealand and Canada.
I am not asking for that reciprocity because I think this should be as of right, but at least in the commonwealth recognition should be given to residence outside. I would go beyond that, of course, and say that a senior citizen should be allowed to reside wherever he or she chooses to reside when the pension is payable. But in any event, even Mr. Bennett as long ago as 1936 spoke of his visit to the Antipodes and the necessity for some arrangement within the commonwealth countries. I thought I would bring that matter to the attention of the minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the government house leader last week cleared the air here to a considerable extent when he made the point that everyone in all parties seemed to agree with the principle of old age pensions, and that he felt we should


be ready to leave the stage where each party is trying to muscle in for its share of the credit or in some cases for all the credit.
In addition, it seems to me that there is quite a large measure of agreement that the scheme threshed out by the 1950 committee and the subsequent legislation have been generally satisfactory. I refer to this idea of the universal scheme, semi-contributory and largely pay as you go. But the key point that bothers me, as the representative of a number of constituents, is the individual sum of money to be paid now or in the future.
I should like to preface my remarks on this matter with two qualifications. The first is a party one. We in this movement feel that there should be an over-all social security program in detail and well thought out, of which old age pensions is only one important facet. Second-and this is more immediate to me as the representative of a constituency-most of my correspondence since June 10, roughly about 75 per cent of it, has dealt with old age pensions, and the key to that correspondence is, "How much?".
People generally seemed to be enraged at the idea of $46 a month. They were thrilled but were not very hopeful at the idea of $100 a month. Most of them seem to feel that somewhere between $65 and $75 would be an ideal figure. Is it possible to get a just pension scheme and set it on some sliding scale that will remove this topic from political promise and counterpromise?
As politicians we should be aware of how fine a thing it would be if we could take this particular issue right out of political controversy.
For example, I imagine the Liberals felt that Mr. Harris with his $46 was being politically courageous, but now they are probably wondering whether he was politically astute. None of us should really want to continue this game of what I call the high-low split. On the face of it the electorate chose the group which had the mystery hole card but that hole card of course has now been revealed to be $55 per month.
The minister who introduced the $55 a month did not state clearly that that was the final figure of his party. He did tell us at page 385 of Hansard that by approving this increase the parliament of Canada will be setting the benefit for our senior citizens at the highest level, both in dollar terms and purchasing power, that it has ever been in the 30-year history of old age pensions in this country. I have looked at the chart which he was kind enough to show me and have compared it with some dominion bureau

of statistics figures and that statement certainly seems to be true. But the minister went on to say:
We make no extravagant claims as to the generosity of the amount we are now proposing. It is my view, rather, that we should try to measure what we are doing here not in terms of generosity but in terms of justice.
This government does not believe that it should try to make a good fellow of itself with the taxpayers' money-
He is changing the tone a little here. The government is not going to be spendthrift with the taxpayers' money. Well, I do not think anyone in this house is going to disagree with these points. We do not want the government to be good fellows with the taxpayers' money and we do want just and fair treatment, but what is the equitable basis in terms of the actual sum these people should get?
The minister went on to make reference to other countries and made comparisons that showed, in relation to the United States and I believe Britain, that we are doing very well or are going to do very well. I noticed in reading back through the speeches of the former minister of health that this was one of his favourite methods, to make a comparison with other countries. I have always felt that there is very little point in such an argument to the old age pensioners themselves. It reminds me of a cook in our regiment who, every time we complained about his cooking, used to say "You think this is bad, but you should have seen what it was like in the last regiment I was in." That is no consolation.
I would like to see if we could get to the point of whether this 1949 figure of $40 was fair at that time. I would like to see the minister table that information in Hansard, and with it I would appreciate it if he would place in another column the figures of the gross national product in those particular years. I would like to know whether the $55 pension is really fair now and whether the government has any means of proving to us or arguing that it is fair. I would like to know whether we should have a flexible pension tied to the cost of living index.
If we could obtain this information exactly we would have a start, because that is the figure which is fundamental in any scale that is sliding. Would a flexible pension tend to freeze our fiscal policy? I think we should find out something about that. The argument of this particular party has been that the pension should be related to the gross national product.
Well, in summing up all these questions I really do not know what should be the exact figure in order to be fair, but I do feel that

it should be higher than $55 per month in view of the pleas of my constituents, and I feel that consideration should be given to the gross national product aspect. I would be the last one to suggest the appointment of another commission, but I would like to see some sort of consideration given to how we can arrive at a just figure to take this whole question of the old age pension figure out of electioneering.
Maybe I am being naive and it should be left in so we could go around playing this kind of game and shouting out the highest or the lowest or the mystery number, but I do think we should try eventually to take this figure out of electioneering.
In conclusion I would like to say that I am most interested in the fact that a social development is taking place with respect to our old age pensioners very much the same as is taking place in the case of teenagers. They seem to be moving out of the family circle or the sort of vertical line within the family and congregating among themselves in various homes, clubs and associations. They are obviously becoming a very powerful pressure group. I think this is good. It seems to me that people with a common interest should form themselves into a pressure group, but we are becoming more and more aware of their power and the sooner we can give this pressure group which, is you might say, improving its pitch, a figure which is generally accepted as being just and fixed to some sort of scale, the better off we will be and the better off they will be.
One last remark in relation to the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. In my particular constituency I would say over half the population has some kind of root in Europe, especially in Finland. I do not know what the general view would be of an ethnic group coming to Canada, making a tremendous contribution in terms of work and development of the backwoods, yet retaining its native language and its ties with the old country. Personally I cannot look down my nose at them for that. I think they have made perhaps the most solid contribution of any group in our area, but many of these people, because they have kept their ties and because they can speak perfect Finnish, do go back to Finland in their old age.
Under the present arrangements we cannot pay their pension, and that is therefore a factor against them. I would support all the other arguments which have been advanced urging that we should wipe out this classification, and I certainly agree that we should obtain figures on how many people

speechtext:
I rise at this time, Mr. Chairman, to speak to this resolution. I would first of all confine myself to the increase of the amount of the old age pension from $46 per month to $55 per month. I am particularly concerned with this problem because I come from the Okanagan Boundary area to which I referred the other day as the California of Canada. We have in that area a large number of old age pensioners who live there because of the beautiful nature of the country and because of its very mild climate.
As members of this house we have no information before us with respect to why the government specifically decided upon the amount of $55 per month. In this house on October 29 I asked a question of the Minister of Finance as to whether the tax revenue of the government in the next 12 months would be equal to or greater than the government's tax revenue in the past 12 months. I did not receive an answer, but the reason I asked that particular question was in order to gain information to help me decide what the specific amount of the old age security pension should be. There is to my knowledge no information at the present time as to how the government decided the amount should be $55 a month.
I think information should be given, particularly to the younger members of this house, as to why that particular amount was decided upon. Why should it not be $60 a month? Personally I would like to see that amount be $60 a month. I realize, of course, that this government has many other responsibilities and that many heavy burdens are cast upon it, but I would like to receive some reasonable answer from the minister as to why this particular amount was decided on. I presume the government takes in sufficient revenue to pay $60 a month? I presume the government's tax revenues are sufficient for this purpose. Let me put it as a question. Are the government's tax revenues sufficient to enable it to pay the old age pensioners the sum of $60 a month? That is the first point I wish to bring to the attention of the committee.
With regard to the second item in the resolution, relating to reducing the period of residence from 20 years to 10 years, I consider this to be a progressive step indeed.
I was surprised personally that the government had been able to reduce the period of residence to this extent. I feel, as does the Minister of National Health and Welfare, that there should be some restriction as to residence, because after all the people of this

country who worked hard to bring about this development, the people who have resided in this country for a number of years, are the ones who should participate in the benefits of old age security. I shall not deal with this point further because I think the government has taken the right course in this regard.
However, I would like to raise a third point which deals with the temporary absence of pensioners from Canada, absences of between three and six months. Under the Old Age Security Act provision is made in section 5, subsection 1, statutes of Canada, 1951 (2nd session) as follows:
Where a pensioner absents himself from Canada, payment of his pension shall be suspended immediately following the payment for the month in which he so absents himself, but may be resumed when the pensioner returns; and where the pensioner returns to Canada within six months from the time he left Canada, the pension upon being resumed may also be paid for a period of such absence not exceeding three months in any calendar year.
That provision has the effect of penalizing the pensioner, and this government did at least see the wisdom of increasing the permitted period of temporary absence from Canada from three months to six months. In that respect, however, I do not feel the government has gone far enough, and I think the best way to explain my point would be by reading from correspondence which has come to my attention. I would like the facts of this matter to be on record in Hansard.
I received a letter, the original of which I have, from an old lady in Cascade, British Columbia. I shall not read it all, but I shall read the relevant part. It is from Mr. and Mrs. J. A. Bertois, dated September 5, 1957, and it reads as follows:
We are old pioneers here, "old and sick people" now, so would like to ask your advice and your help. Mr. Bertois is 84, November 1-lived here 64 years at Cascade. I am 77 November 27 and have lived here 59 years last March. We have been in many businesses and have paid a lot of taxes. I got my back hurt in a car accident last fall, so I can't take care of my invalid husband alone any longer. He has had hardening of the
arteries for 12 years-getting worse every year_
and now can't take a step alone, and with my bad back I can't hold him up. So I want to ask you and the government if you could arrange some way to let us live with our daughter in Los Angeles permanently-
The word "permanently" is underlined.
-and our pension cheques-
Those words, too, have been underlined.
-mailed to us there. That would be heavenly for us.
There were rumours that such arrangements would be made, or should be made, so very old pensioners could go and let the children take care of their old and sick parents.

Then later on I received a further letter from the same lady at Cascade, dated September 14, 1957, in which she said:
Your very kind letter and copy was received, but now we have had real bad news. Mr. E. A. McGovern, our son in law at 1148 South Plymouth, Los Angeles, California, was in a car accident and the following day died in the veterans' hospital at Los Angeles and is now buried. Why this terrible thing should happen, God only knows.
Now our dear daughter is alone and needs us, as much as we need her, so as soon as we can possibly get lined up we must go to her. Our daughter is a Vancouver General hospital graduate, R.N. also a United States R.N. So she is such a help and comfort to us in dear dad's sickness, and now she also needs us to comfort her.
Mr. Chairman, I was very much pleased when I read of the resolution which was passed by the senior citizens' association of British Columbia at its fourth annual convention held on June 3 and 4, 1957. This was the resolution:
Resolved that this convention of the senior citizens' association of British Columbia requests the federal government to amend the Old Age Security and Old Age Assistance Acts to make it possible for the pensioner to receive his pension in any country in the world.
I appreciate that steps are being taken to improve the situation so far as temporary absences are concerned, but I feel it should be a matter of right that our older citizens should have that individual freedom to which they are entitled, and that in the latter days of their lives they should be able to reside wherever they please and wherever they can receive the greatest comfort and attention. I therefore bring this matter respectfully to the attention of the government and express the hope that they will consider what can be done.
All hon. members will agree, I am sure, that it is most important we should pay fair and realistic pensions to the senior citizens of this country.

Mr. Chairman, 1 am sure it is a pleasure for me to speak on this resolution regarding old age pensions. There are a few points I would like to bring out in support of this bill. Surely none of us would deny the maximum amount of assistance to these old people, in keeping with the ability of this country to pay.
Let us examine a few of the facts. First, the savings of the great majority of these people have been severely deflated over the last several years, necessitating, the depletion of the purchasing power of these savings. The other observation I would make is that those savings were compiled when they had to work a 10-hour day six days a week to earn as much as is earned in an hour today. All of this we have to consider, and
Old Age Security Act
we should realize, too, that those people laid the foundation for what we are enjoying in this great country today.
That fact, I believe, was partially expressed or conceded by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano when he suggested that the government had perhaps not taken this fact fully into account when it provided a 15 per cent increase.
Now let us take a look at the housing and food factors. Since 1950 food has increased 22 per cent in price; housing has increased 36 per cent. Our proposed increase is 37J per cent, which allows us a little leeway, and only a very little, I admit, to look after the loss through deflation of those senior citizens' savings. So I believe our legislation has been realistic. I am sure all of us on this side of the house feel it is not enough, but economic factors must also be taken into consideration.
Furthermore, I have this to add. More of us will be living to 70 which is the life expectancy now for children born in this era, and it necessarily follows that we will have an ageing population on our hands. It also follows that more of these people will necessarily be employed in the older age groups than ever before.
I must say a few words on the cutting down of the residence from 20 years to 10 years as applied to immigrants to this country. I think that is a very necessary move, and I believe anyone who opposes this has lost sight of a very basic factor in that the great majority of those people will be healthy, young people right at the start of their working careers. Some of them will be skilled, others will not be, but let us consider this fact. We have put no care or costs into these people. We have paid them no baby bonuses. We have paid no hospitalization, no medical fees, nor payments for education for their bread and butter from the time they were born. We did not even pay for the mother's hospitalization or prenatal care.
As a matter of fact we are being handed a large sum of money already invested in those people, and this sum is estimated at from $20,000 to $200,000, depending upon the skill and training of these people. For those very few who come in under other circumstances- and there will be a few-we would be just as far ahead to give them this pension as to look after them in form of relief.
In conclusion may I say we have approached this Old Age Assistance Act with sympathy, realistically looking at all the factors that have to do with this legislation under consideration at the present time.

There has been some discussion here this morning with respect to arriving at a particular figure for social assistance, which includes this resolution which we have before us. I would like to suggest that in arriving at a figure of social assistance in respect of any of these matters the total amount of consumer goods available in Canada, taking into account our productivity and our ability as individuals to consume goods and services, would give us a sound basis on which we could judge whether we can pay so much here or so much there, because in our opinion if it is going to be continually based on dollars and cents we shall not arrive at a basis of the amount of goods and services we actually have available to divide amongst our people in a way which will give our senior citizens the standard of living they require.

Last night the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount referred to a report in the Toronto Daily Star of April 25 concerning a speech made by the Prime Minister in Toronto and said, as reported at page 625 of Hansard:
I therefore want to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, the fact that there were three points in this promise. First, the payments would be high enough to meet the needs of the recipients. Second, the payments would be adjusted from time to time to keep pace with increases in the cost of living. Third, the payments would be geared to national productivity.
Well, if I might point out, Mr. Chairman, we are raising the pension to $55 monthly and that, in our judgment, constitutes a fair and reasonable level of benefit at the present time. It will be sufficient in our judgment, together with the other means that most pensioners have at their disposal, to provide a decent minimum level of living for most pensioners.
In raising the pension to $55 a month we are increasing it to a figure 37.5 per cent in excess of the $40 level which prevailed at the first of the year. The cost of living index, by comparison, has risen only 23 per cent since 1949, and only 5 per cent since 1952 when old age security payments commenced.
In raising the pension to $55 a month we are in fact increasing it to keep in step with national productivity. This was the third of the points referred to by the hon. member last night in his remarks concerning the Prime Minister's speech. Here are the facts and figures in support of my contention, Mr. Chairman. In 1952, when old age security began, the gross national product was $23i billion. In 1957 it had risen to an estimated $30.8 billion, according to latest figures. This increase amounts to 32.4 per cent, and during the same period the increase in pension level amounts to 37.5 per cent.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this shows clearly that on the three points referred to in the Prime Minister's speech we have met our commitment. One, we have raised pensions by this proposal to a fair and reasonable level. Two, we have adjusted it by these proposals for the cost of living increase since old age security began. Three, we have adjusted by these proposals for the increase in national productivity as reflected in the gross national product since old age security began in 1952.
I think this question was asked. What did I think of the fund raised by the 2-2-2 formula? I personally do not consider it a contributory scheme, certainly not in the full

sense of the word. I know there are arguments for and against, but the amount required each year has never been met by that formula. The amount has varied. The last complete picture is, I think, that it did come fairly close to meeting it prior to the recent rise and the one proposed right now; but actually, because of the demand on the consolidated revenue fund, I have not considered this actually was a fully contributory scheme.
If there are any other specific questions at the moment I will answer them, but I still think it would be advisable to get the bill and proceed with second reading.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE, RESIDENCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution preceding the introduction of the amendments proposed to the Old Age Assistance Act includes three main points. They are as follows:
1.	A proposal to share with the provinces, if they agree, a further increase of the maximum amount of old age assistance bringing the figure to $55 monthly, the same as for old age security.
2.	A proposed reduction in the basic residence requirement from 20 to 10 years.
3.	A proposed increase in the income ceilings covering both the assistance payable and the amount of outside income by $120 annually in the case of unmarried recipients and $240 annually in the case of recipients of married status.
The considerations which prompted the government to propose the first two of these three changes are almost exactly the same as those which were discussed in connection with the resolution on the Old Age Security Act amendments. I do not propose to repeat the arguments which I advanced in that debate. I might point out however that there are obvious advantages in terms of administrative efficiency and convenience to the recipients in having the pension payable under old age assistance before the age of 70 identical with that paid after 70. Certainly if it is desirable to raise the benefits under old age security to $55, and we all agree that it is, we can hardly do less for old age assistance recipients between the ages of 65 and 70, all of whom by definition are in need of assistance to a greater extent than many of those in receipt of old age security.
A comparison of the maximum amount of old age assistance now proposed with that paid in other countries shows that the Canadian level of benefits once these changes have been approved will be higher than those of every other country except the United States and will not lag far behind the rates payable in that country. United States legislation with respect to old age assistance provides for federal sharing of state administered old


age assistance payments, paid on a means test basis, up to a maximum of $60 monthly. In fact, because of the means test the actual average payments amount to less than $60 a month. There were actually 15 state or territorial jurisdictions which in June 1957 were making average assistance payments of less than $50 monthly while eight were in the $50 to $55 range and 30 were in excess of $55.
I mention these figures as they apply to the United States in order that we may all have a clear understanding as to where we stand in comparison with our neighbour to the south. With the exceptions I have noted in respect to some of the individual states the new $55 maximum proposed for Canada compares favourably with anything to be found in other jurisdictions.
I should of course add that while the federal government is asking parliament to authorize these changes in our joint federal-provincial program of old age assistance, the provincial governments will in the final analysis be the ones to decide whether or not these changes are to be made in their respective jurisdictions. No changes in old age assistance can be made effective in any province except as and when the province itself may decide. We are however making it clear to the provinces by the proposed amended legislation that, so far as the federal government is concerned, we are prepared with parliament's approval to amend the existing federal-provincial agreements and to share henceforth in the cost of a maximum $55 assistance payment.
The second change proposed in the Old Age Assistance Act has to do with the reduction of the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years. There is nothing I need to add on this subject to what I said when we were considering an identical proposal for the Old Age Security Act. The arguments and the considerations are identical. I might just add that we have already received representations from at least one province, Ontario, urging this reduction to 10 years and we have every reason to believe that the change will be acceptable to the other provinces as well.
The third change proposed for old age assistance relates to the income ceilings provided under the act. Since this is a means test program certain limits must be placed on the amount of income and resources which an applicant can have without reduction of the amount of assistance payable to him. For every dollar of income in excess of the permitted amount a corresponding reduction is made in the amount of assistance paid.
The increase of $9 monthly, or $108 yearly, in the amount of assistance payable necessitates a corresponding adjustment in the

overall income ceilings. If this were not done many of those in receipt of modest amounts of outside income would not receive the full benefit of the increase which is proposed. It is for this reason that the government has decided to propose an increase of $120 annually in the income ceiling for unmarried recipients and an increase of $240 annually in the ceiling for married recipients.
I come now to the financial implications of these three proposals. I must be frank in admitting that these are difficult to assess with accuracy for a number of reasons. The first of these is that despite the growing numbers of our population in the age brackets 65 to 70 the experience in the last few years has been that the old age assistance rolls have not risen in proportion. There has in fact been a decline from 94,625 in March, 1955 to 88,887 in June of this year.
Some slight increase has resulted from the changes made in the early part of this year but with other programs such as war veterans allowances, disability or blindness allowances and unemployment insurance, providing alternative benefits for many persons in the age group 65 to 70, it becomes increasingly difficult to estimate how many additional persons may qualify for old age assistance as a result of alterations in the rate of benefit or in the income ceilings. At the present time there are approximately 90,000 persons in receipt of old age assistance in the provinces and territories.

Approximately 90,000. All these will qualify for the full increase of $9 per month and the increased costs on this count alone will amount to about $9| million per annum. In addition, some increase in case-load is anticipated as a result of the higher rate of benefits, the increase in income ceilings and the reduction in the residence requirement. Possibly this will mean an additional 5,000 cases a month; if so, the cost of these would be an additional $3.3 million as a maximum.
Summing up, therefore, it may be anticipated that old age assistance costs will rise as a result of these amendments by approximately $13 million which is in a full fiscal year. Half of this sum or $6.5 million will be a federal responsibility; the rest will be a charge upon the provincial treasuries.
May I say a word in conclusion about the position of the provincial government in this matter. We have, of course, notified all the governments concerned of the proposals that we are laying before parliament as embodied in these resolutions. We shall send them copies of the bill for their consideration at
Old Age Assistance Act the earliest possible moment, that is to say as soon as it has been introduced and given first reading in this house.
The federal government fully recognizes that in amending its own legislation, the federal Old Age Assistance Act, it cannot and does not legislate for the provinces. It can only indicate in this way to the provinces what it is prepared to do. The provinces must in their turn decide, each one in the light of its own position, the extent to which they can incorporate into their provincial legislation and program the changes and improvements in which the federal government, through these amendments, is announcing its readiness to share.
If all ten provinces decide to implement these changes, and there can be no certainty of that until they have had the time to consider the matter, the added burden on the provincial treasuries will amount to about $6 million a year. They will also have to bear their share of any increases under disability and blindness allowances. It may take a little time for all the provinces to consider their position and come to a decision with respect to these three acts. It may also be necessary in one or two jurisdictions to effect changes in provincial legislation before these improvements can be legally made effective. New agreements with all the provinces will be required; this alone can mean as many as 36 new agreements-three each with the 10 provinces and two territories.
The committee can be assured that the federal government will expedite by all the means at its disposal the conclusions of the necessary agreements. That is why we have provided in the bill for an effective date November 1, 1957. But the position of the provinces, and the problems, financial and other, which the federal legislation poses for them should not be minimized. They should be clearly understood, and it should be recognized that the provinces will require a reasonable amount of time to come to their decisions and to make the necessary policy and administrative decisions in the matter. I am sure the committee will recognize the fairness of this position.
I think that is about all I need to say at this stage, Mr. Chairman. I shall be glad to deal with any points that may arise as the debate proceeds, to the best of my ability.

Mr. Chairman, I would naturally, I think, be expected to make a few remarks based on the statement we have just heard from the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the introduction of this particular amendment which, in fact, is an amendment to Bill No. 395 introduced in this parliament on June 23, 1951.
Of course I agree at once with what the minister has just said about our responsibility in relation to that which can be exercised by the provinces, and I am sure that it was only because the hon. member for Fort William sometimes suffers from a particular disability of hearing that he did not appreciate the point which was properly made by the minister when he said that acceptance of this measure and its availability to the public generally depended on agreement between the provinces on one hand and the federal government on the other, and the practice to which he has resorted in passing enabling legislation is a practice which we, when we were on this side of the house, always followed notwithstanding the criticisms made when old age pensions were first introduced, and that is that before the federal government embarked on any legislative enactments having to do with participation by the provinces, the latter should first of all have given their consent and enacted the necessary legislation. I agree with the practice which the hon. gentleman is pursuing in this particular instance.
This particular measure is, as I say, by way of amendment to an act introduced by the government headed by the right hon. gentleman who is now the Leader of the Opposition. That was in 1951, and it was part of a plan which had first been proposed in 1945 and considered later by the parliamentary committee which recommended that there should be a lowering of the pensionable age, the federal government assuming responsibility basically, pursuant to a constitutional amendment, for those aged 70 and over.
Now I think it is significant that in the very terms of the constitutional amendment itself the provinces were not turning over to the federal government full responsibility


for old age pensions but they were endowing the federal government with the necessary authority to impose contributions in respect of a particular program covering the group aged 70 and over, and I think that is very important because it has much to do with an argument that I am going to sug-get to the minister, that is that it would be most unfortunate if as a result of those amendments any provinces now paying supplementary payments were to take the position that in view of these increased benefits they were thereby relieved of any responsibility. I suggest to the minister, not without some reason, that that is a possibility he should look into, as I am sure he will, with the greatest care.
Now as a result of the act of June 23, 1951 parliament took a very important step. Hitherto pensions had been paid on the basis of co-operative financial participation between the federal government and provincial governments and once the federal government assumed responsibility within certain limits for over 800,000 people in this country aged 70 years and over it decided to lower the age for a particular group, but that the provinces and the federal government should share on a fifty-fifty basis the benefits provided under the Old Age Assistance Act, which provided for these benefits to be paid at the age of 65 instead of at the age of 70.
It is significant I think that up until 1951 over 800,000 Canadians have benefited under the Old Age Pensions Act which was made possible as the result of the cost being shared by the two senior levels of government.
It is worth recording that up to 1951 the federal and provincial governments had spent together $1,136 millions by way of assistance to the senior citizens of our country. I have checked these contributions up to date with contributions made on a proportional basis-a per capita basis-in the United States, to which the hon. gentleman properly made allusion a few moments ago, and it will be found that we have provided more assistance on a per capita basis to our older citizens, certainly up to 1951, than they have in the United States, out of contributions made by the taxpayers pursuant to policies carried out by the government.
Of this sum of $1,136 million which had been spent in the period before the introduction of the Old Age Assistance Act, federal expenditure alone amounted to $836 million, while provincial expenditures were in the neighbourhood of $300 million. Therefore, this amendment is based upon an act which came into effect after a very considerable contribution had been made by the

taxpayers, pursuant to government policy, to help the senior citizens of our country.
Now the Old Age Assistance Act, unlike the Old Age Security Act, apart altogether from supplementary payments, is now made possible, if accepted by the provinces, on a sharing basis with the latter. I think it is important at this stage that we should state that the operation and the administration of this act which presumably will, as in the past, be left to the provinces, require for proper administration regulations between the two senior levels of government, jointly entered into and jointly collaborated in.
I am going to suggest to my hon. friend that he will be confronted with the difficulty that I was confronted with so very frequently in this house when it was suggested that the regulations attending old age assistance were not mutually agreed upon but rather imposed on from the top. My hon. friend knows, of course, that that is not the case. The regulations in the past-and I am sure this will be true of the future-were the result of consideration by the two senior levels of government on equal terms, and at no conference that I ever participated in were any of these regulations at any time imposed from the top or from the provinces. They were the result of mutual argeement. Certainly the provinces which have to administer this act would naturally be expected to have a great deal to say and an important part to play in the administration, in the creation and in the formation of those particular regulations.
When the Old Age Assistance Act was introduced in 1951 for the 65 to 69 age group we intended to embrace almost one-third of the population in that age group. Our estimate at that time was that we were going to cover 145,000 persons but, as the minister has pointed out today by way of implication, we did not reach that figure. I think some 90,000 persons roughly were covered and as a result of these amendments undoubtedly further numbers will be added.
It is significant that prior to the introduction of the Old Age Assistance Act-and this has much to do with this act because of the increase in the permissible income ceiling- there were at least three different amendments made in the availability of permissible income. The basic amount had been increased. As a matter of fact, to indicate the scope of the contribution made by this measure one can note that the cost of old age pensions was doubled between 1947 and the date when the Old Age Assistance Act was first introduced.
"It is also significant that under the act to which my hon. friend now presents an
Old Age Assistance Act amendment not only had we previously increased the basic amount, not only had we liberalized the income ceilings but we had in the act of 1951, of which this is now an integral proposed part, taken some very important steps and made some very important changes. For instance, the residence requirements were liberalized; the requirement of citizenship was completely eliminated. That represented a very significant change. Hitherto it was based entirely upon citizenship and period of residence. In the act of 1951 that was removed and, as a matter of fact, all of our social measures now are not based upon national status but on the period of residence, and that had the effect of bringing in many thousands of people who came from other lands to participate in Canadian citizenship and all of the advantages which this country affords.
Now, the basic amount of $40, the qualifying law, the maintenance of an eligibility test are all embodied in the act of which the amendment offered by the hon. gentleman is a part and were all recommended by the parliamentary committee. It is significant that many hon. members who now sit on Mr. Chairman's right, complained bitterly when this act was introduced about the maintenance of the eligibility test. I use the phrase "eligibility test" to get away from the implications and the sinister quality of the old designation. But there are many hon. members sitting opposite who took a strong position in 1951 and who said that the act was made to appear very weak because it did not propose the abolition of the eligibility test. There were the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and the former leader of the opposition. All of these men will be found to be on record as strongly taking the position that there should not be in this measure any eligibility test.
I merely mention that to indicate that what was the view of hon. gentlemen opposite at one time is apparently not the view which they entertain today. In the light of the serious and severe criticism that was carried on for many, many days in this house, I think it is important that one should recall the position taken now as compared with the position taken then.

Old Age Assistance Act at the legislation that has been passed in this field by the preceding government. He will find that it is a record worthy of commendation and worthy of praise rather than the kind of criticism sometimes given to it.
Then in the act of 1951 we took another step; we eliminated the requirement of the recovery from the estates of deceased persons in so far as the federal government is concerned. I am sure my hon. friend is going to maintain that. We cannot control what the provinces do in that particular, but it is significant that we did make that change in the act. Then we introduced a new feature in the act of 1951 of which this amendment is a part. We gave to the Indians, to the native population of our country, the right to benefit, something that had not been done before.
We estimated the total cost of old age assistance in 1951 at about $64 million, shared equally by the two senior levels of government and I understood my hon. friend to estimate that the proposed amendments would add roughly another $13 million, to be shared equally by the two senior levels of government, bringing the total cost of old age assistance to somewhere between $75 million and $80 million.
So we can support this particular proposal in the knowledge that this is an amendment to an act which we introduced. Undoubtedly it has been made possible as the result of the minister's careful concept of the overall obligations having in mind, I sincerely hope-I know he will not mind my saying this-that this does not mean in any way any postponement or abridgment of the plan proposed by the previous government in the matter of hospital insurance.

No, I think in fairness to the Minister of National Health and Welfare I should mention that I did say in the house that when he took office he was the one member of the administration who had given a clear indication of his personal intentions in that regard. He will recall the statement I made several weeks ago that my complaint was that he was

the sole voice on behalf of the administration that gave any indication that the government intended to carry on vigorously the purposes and intentions embodied in the hospital insurance act. His statement now relieves us from any suspicion that what is now being done is in any way intended to be considered as postponing the day when Canadians generally will have the opportunity to participate in a nationwide hospital insurance scheme.
Of course the amendment now proposed does not deal, as the previous amendment did not deal, with certain assurances or certain promises, as the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount said last night, that were made in the election that not only would the basic amount be increased but there would be a formula provided to relate the pension to the cost of living. I want to say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that there has never been a refinement as to precisely what was meant by those assurances, and I think that if they are going to be realized there should be some guarantee given with respect to the great danger of a reduction in pension if there is a reduction in the cost of living.
An examination of social security measures in other countries based upon such a formula will show that in times of less need there have been reductions in social benefits away below the actual reduction in the cost of living itself. Therefore this formula which was dealt with on the basis of an assurance should be considered with great care. In any event, I take it that particular promise is not going to be recognized in this legislation. Likewise the assurance about relating payments or benefits to the gross national product is not being presented in this particular amendment.
We should keep in perspective what the over-all obligation of the government of Canada is in the whole matter of assistance to our senior citizens. Before the amendments introduced last spring in the budget of that time the federal government had committed the people of Canada to an expenditure of something like $400 million for old age security, including the contributions that the federal government was paying to the provinces under the Old Age Assistance Act. The increases provided at that time resulted in a total commitment of $460 million, and with the proposed amendments now our share of old age security will bring us to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $560 million. This is comparable with the amount of roughly $35 million now being spent by all ten of the provinces together apart from supplementary payments.

It is for this reason that I strongly suggest to the minister, having in mind the fact that the federal government bears a much greater share in this regard than all the provinces to the extent that I have indicated, $560 million as against $35 million, that it would be a matter for great regret in terms of the value of social measures if as a result of these amendments the provinces were now to seek to extricate themselves from some of the supplementary payment obligations into which some of them have projected themselves.
As I indicated the other day, there are five at least that do not make any supplementary payments. It would be unfortunate if this legislation meant that supplementary payments would not be continued or that discouragement would be given to provinces where there are no supplementary payments now because this amount will not take care of all cases of need. I am sure my hon. friend recognizes that is the case, and the only way in a country like ours by which individual cases of need can be met is by the provinces recognizing that they too have a responsibility in this matter. I am sure the hon. gentleman will find that we will give the bill the same sympathetic consideration as we have given its antecedent.

can be left to some future occasion. The C.C.F. party's approach to the question of old age assistance can be generally summed up by our belief that the age limit of those in receipt of old age security should be lowered
Old Age Assistance Act to age 65. If that were done we would not now be faced with the situation described by the minister where he has no assurance or guarantee that certain provinces are going to enter into agreements with the federal government to provide for a pension of $55 to recipients of old age assistance.
The situation we are likely to find in the immediate future is that the amount of old age assistance will vary from one part of the country to the other. I feel that all our senior citizens, irrespective of the province of residence, should be given equal treatment. I realize that the minister can point the finger at a specific province and say the province did not fulfil its obligation and that is the reason why some of our senior citizens are not accorded the same treatment as their fellow Canadians are in some other part of the country.
At this point I might say I was quite surprised to hear the hon. member for Essex East express a great deal of concern over the question of supplementary allowances. I think it would be much more advisable for him to express a little more concern about those provinces that do not give any supplementary allowance. I suggest his great concern over the provinces who grant supplementary allowances is because of the fact that there is not a single Liberal province in the dominion which has given or is now giving any supplementary allowance to the recipients of old age pensions. I would suggest the hon. member for Essex East should go to work on the few remaining Liberal provinces, while there are still a few remaining, to convince them it may be well to play fair with the old age pensioners residing within those provinces.
I noted that in the remarks made in a previous debate one Liberal member suggested that the provinces were not making the same contribution as was the federal government. I think he overlooked the fact that the provincial governments are much closer to the problems of our senior citizens. They are charged with the responsibility of providing medical care; they are charged with the responsibility of providing suitable housing and satisfying other basic requirements. This is a field in which the province is concerned. I know that in my own province the amount which we spend as our share of the payments under the Old Age Assistance Act is only a part of the amount which the provincial government spends in the care of our senior citizens.
As a matter of fact on September 25 I had the great pleasure of attending the opening of our new geriatric and rehabilitation centre in the city of Regina. This is an

Old Age Assistance Act indication of the sort of thing that is being done by some provincial governments and, of course, that is over and above any money they spend in providing assistance under the Old Age Assistance Act. This new geriatric centre was built at a total cost of over $2,133,000 and has provision for 293 guests. It has a staff of around 130, including the superintendent, 20 registered nurses, 56 nursing assistants and the other staff members required to operate a home of that kind.
The provincial government has undertaken this work because they feel it is necessary that the legitimate needs of our senior citizens be met. I am very sorry that we have not been able to go much farther in this field. I think perhaps the provincial government could devote its energy toward the provision of care of this kind because there are so many of our senior citizens who do not have homes, whose families are not living in this country or perhaps are unable to provide for them the sort of care that is necessary. I suggest, therefore, when the federal government is bringing in an amendment of this kind they should take into consideration the fact that the provincial governments-I am not saying all provincial governments to an equal degree or measure -have been doing a great deal in this direction. I feel that this work should be continued.
I feel that the amendment now before us, which carries on the old arrangement whereby the cost of old age assistance is to be borne jointly by the federal and provincial governments, does not take into account sufficiently what is being done by the provincial governments toward the care of our senior citizens. If the government insists on taking care of the 65 to 69 age group in this manner, then it ought to face up to some of its responsibilities in other fields.
Some reference has been made to the hospital plan. There is no doubt that the coming into force of that plan, which I presume is a step towards a comprehensive health insurance plan, will be of some assistance. But in the province of Saskatchewan we have been waiting year after year for the federal government to do something. We feel that as a province we are ready to go ahead with the hospital plan now. I should like very much to see this government take the necessary steps in order that Saskatchewan and any other province that is ready may enter into an agreement to bring the plan into effect as of January 1 next. That is one positive way in which the federal government could discharge, in part, some of its responsibilities towards those in the 65


to 69 age group, apart from the contribution they are making under this proposed amendment.
Again, there is the provision of housing for our senior citizens. While I realize there is a limited amount of assistance provided under federal legislation, the bulk of the cost of building homes for our senior citizens rests with the provincial governments, with the municipalities and the societies set up to build such accommodation. Here is another field in which the federal government, if it is going to boast about its accomplishments, if it is going to fully discharge its responsibilities towards the 65 to 69 age group, ought tc do something.
Then, of course, there is the question of our geriatric centres, which I believe to be indispensable to any worthwhile program for our senior citizens in this country. What responsibility is the federal government going to take with respect to the provision of facilities of this kind? I draw this to the attention of the minister because I feel there is an attitude which has been evidenced by members on the Liberal side of the house when they were in office, and that is that because the federal government is paying a portion of the cost under the Old Age Assistance Act they have discharged their responsibility. I cannot agree with that. I feel that the best solution to the difficulty would be to lower the age group in which payments are made under the Old Age Security Act. Mr. Chairman, may I first of all say to you, as this is the first time I have spoken in the house with you in the chair, that I should like at this very late date to congratulate one who has been for so many years in the house on his appointment as deputy chairman of the committees of the house.
I should like to make a few brief comments on thfe measure as I have with regard to the others because, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare well knows, this too, like its companion predecessors, is an amendment to an act of parliament introduced by the previous administration. It is interesting to note that the opposition to old age pensions which first emanated in the other place in 1926 was based in part upon the fact that the pension was given to old people just as a matter of right instead of being given to persons who were incapacitated. Indeed, that was the position taken by the then leader of the opposition in this house, Mr. Meighen, and others who spoke on that measure. So the blind were covered up to a point only in so far as they came within the definition of the phrase "old age" under the Old Age Pensions Act until 1937 when amendments to that act were provided to include the blind in a specific way.
It is a matter of history that between 1937 and 1951 the basic amount of pensions to the blind was increased and so were the ceilings on permissible outside income. In my hon. friend's recital today of the income ceilings provided by this amendment he has adhered to the standard of previous amendments in that these income ceilings are higher than the income ceilings in the two preceding measures.

In 1951 the act of which this is an amendment provided for a separate measure to cover the blind. The Canadian National Institute for the Blind in particular and some hon. members had repeatedly urged that instead of covering the blind under the Old Age Pensions Act they should be provided for under an act especially designated for the blind themselves. So it was a historic step in 1951 when we enacted a separate measure covering the blind, a measure to which my hon. friend has now provided an acceptable amendment.
The act of 1951 brought the benefits to an additional 3,000 blind persons, a total altogether, if we include those who were provided for under the Old Age Security Act, of roughly
15,000	persons. I think it is noteworthy in considering this amendment that when we brought in the Blind Persons Act of 1951 we gave effect to the requests made by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. They had put forward a six point program and every one of those points was given accession to by the act introduced by the government headed by the present Leader of the Opposition. These six points can be found for reference in Hansard of June 23, 1951, at page 4589 and following.
As the result of that act we liberalized the eligibility tests very considerably, bringing in numbers of blind persons who otherwise would not have been included because of the regulations, and it is significant that we reduced the qualifying age from 20 to 10 years in the act of which the amendment is now proposed to be a part.
In addition, I think it should be recognized that this is by no means all that the people of Canada through the government are doing for the blind people of Canada. Under departmental estimates, which I am sure my hon. friend would not disturb, the federal government has undertaken to pay 75 per cent of surgical operation expenses in eye operations. The result has been, as I am sure my hon. friend has now been able to ascertain from an examination of the departmental records, that we have provided for the complete rehabilitation of over 50 per cent of the blind persons to whom this financial assistance for eye surgery has been provided. That has not only given these people a restoration of eyesight but it has at the same time lessened the numbers who are on the pension rolls.
This is a program of rehabilitation in which, if I may say so, I have a special interest and it is one which I know the minister will want to carry on. The federal government pays 75 per cent of the cost of that scheme, the provinces paying only 25 per
